summaries.example: Imagine seeing a bright red kite. Consciousness is the way the kite looks to you—the experience you have. Intentionality is what your mind is focused on: the kite. If you remember the kite later, your thought is still about it, even though it is no longer in front of you. Philosophers ask whether the experience and the aboutness are separate or closely connected.
summaries.summary: Consciousness and intentionality are two broad features of mental life. Consciousness concerns having experiences: there is some way it feels or appears to be in a state, such as seeing a color, feeling pain, remembering an event, or becoming angry. Intentionality concerns what a mental state is about or directed toward. A person can think about a friend, want a new bicycle, imagine a dragon, or remember a meeting. These mental states have intentionality even when their objects are absent or imaginary. The entry explains that both ideas are difficult to define. Philosophers disagree about whether thoughts, perceptions, and feelings all count as experiences in the same sense. They also disagree about what makes a mental state represent something and how representation works when the thing represented is false or nonexistent. The central question is how consciousness and intentionality fit together. Separatists treat felt experience and aboutness as different. Intentionalists say that conscious experience necessarily includes some kind of aboutness, or that its felt character can be explained through representation. Some intentionalist views connect experience to the outside world, while others emphasize what happens within the subject. Other debates ask whether perception and action have a basic kind of understanding before words and concepts, and whether consciousness includes a quiet awareness of itself or of the person having it. These questions affect how we understand minds, knowledge, the self, and value.
key_ideas: Conscious experiences include seeing, hearing, imagining, remembering, thinking, and feeling emotions.
Intentionality is the mind’s aboutness. A thought can be about something real, something imagined, or something that does not exist.
Philosophers disagree about whether consciousness and intentionality are separate or whether one helps explain the other.
Some philosophers think conscious experience depends on the world and the body; others think it could remain much the same even if the outside world changed.
Consciousness may include simple sensing, practical bodily understanding, thinking, or awareness of oneself, depending on the theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic helps us ask what makes a mind different from an object that only carries information, such as a sign or a computer file. It also helps explain how we know things through seeing and feeling, how we know our own thoughts, and why experiences may matter to us. Understanding these ideas can make everyday questions about thinking, learning, perception, and personal identity clearer.

important_terms.definition: The part of mental life that gives an experience a felt or experienced quality—what seeing red or feeling pain is like for you.
The mind’s being about, focused on, or directed toward something, such as an object, event, idea, or imagined place.
The particular way an experience feels or appears to the person having it.
The idea that a thought, feeling, or perception points toward something or represents it in the mind.

questions_to_think_about: Can a thought be about something that does not exist?
Is feeling pain the same kind of thing as thinking about pain?
Could a person have a mind without having any experiences?
When you notice your own thought, are you having a new thought about the first one?

summaries.example: Suppose two students look at a shaded object. One sees it as a familiar chair; the other, distracted and uncertain, sees only a shape. Their sensory input may be similar, but their experiences could differ in what the object appears to be. A philosopher might ask whether this difference is a difference in phenomenal character, intentional content, or both. Another question is whether a hallucination of a chair shares an important mental feature with genuinely seeing a chair, or whether genuine perception is essentially a relation to the real object.
summaries.summary: The entry examines two central features of mind. Phenomenal consciousness concerns subjective experience: seeing a color, feeling pain, imagining a scene, recalling an event, entertaining a thought, or undergoing an emotion all seem to have a way they are experienced. Intentionality concerns mental directedness or content: beliefs, desires, perceptions, intentions, and imaginings are about objects, properties, events, or situations. The two notions are difficult partly because their boundaries are disputed. Some philosophers distinguish phenomenal consciousness from access consciousness, in which information is available for reasoning and action, and from monitoring consciousness, in which a subject represents its own mental states. Some deny that all these uses name genuine kinds of consciousness. Intentionality is equally contested. It may be understood as reference to an object, as having conditions under which a state is true, accurate, or fulfilled, or as possessing representational content. These approaches must explain false beliefs, fictional objects, hallucinations, and the difference between thinking of an object under one description and another. The historical discussion contrasts phenomenological approaches, which begin with first-person experience and practical engagement with the world, with analytic approaches shaped by logic, language, and theories of mental content. The main contemporary dispute is between separatism and intentionalism. Separatists treat phenomenal character as distinct from intentionality. Intentionalists claim that phenomenal character entails, consists in, or is otherwise tied to representational content. Intentionalist views differ over whether content depends on the environment, whether consciousness can be reduced to nonconscious
key_ideas: Phenomenal consciousness, access to information, and monitoring of one’s own states are often distinguished, but philosophers disagree about whether these are genuinely different kinds of consciousness.
Intentionality can be analyzed through directedness, conditions of satisfaction, or content. Each approach faces problems involving error, hallucination, fiction, and nonexistent objects.
Phenomenological philosophers emphasize first-person experience, perceptual constancy, practical bodily engagement, and the relation between consciousness and self-awareness.
Analytic philosophers often approach intentionality through language, logic, mental content, and the internalism-externalism debate; later work reconnects these issues with consciousness.
Intentionalist theories vary: they may be externalist or internalist, reductive or non-reductive, restrictive or inclusive, and reflexivist or non-reflexivist.

The richness of consciousness is disputed. Questions include whether perception represents high-level properties, whether experience has fine detail, and whether thought has a distinctive phenomenology.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates shape theories of what minds and selves are, where the boundaries of the mental lie, and whether consciousness is necessary for genuine thought. They also affect theories of perception and justification: if experience has intentional or even conceptual content, it may help support knowledge rather than merely cause beliefs. The debates matter to self-knowledge because they ask how we become aware of our own states. Finally, they influence theories of value, including whether conscious experience has non-instrumental value and whether persons’ value depends essentially on their continuing experience.

important_terms.definition: Consciousness understood as having an experience with a subjective character: there is something it is like for the subject to be in the state.
The aboutness, reference, or directedness of mental states toward objects, events, properties, or states of affairs.
The way a mental state represents something as being, including what is thought, perceived, desired, or imagined.
A position claiming that phenomenal consciousness necessarily involves some form of intentionality or representation.
A position separating phenomenal experience from intentionality, treating felt qualities as not essentially representational.
The view that a mental state’s content depends partly on relations to the external world, body, or linguistic community.
The question of whether consciousness is essentially related to its own states or to the self as subject, without requiring reflective thought.
The dispute over whether thinking and understanding have their own distinctive experiential character beyond sensory imagery or sensation.

questions_to_think_about: Does a hallucination have the same intentional content as genuine perception, or is genuine perception essentially object-dependent?
Could two experiences represent the same property while differing in phenomenal character?
Does understanding a sentence change what the experience is like, beyond changes in sound or imagery?
If a conscious state must be represented by another mental state, how can a regress of representations be avoided?
Would a being with no subjective experience still have beliefs, knowledge, or value?

summaries.example: You are reading a mystery novel and picture a hidden city. Your imagination is conscious because it has a felt quality: perhaps you can picture the streets or feel suspense. It also has intentionality because it is about the city and the story. The city may be fictional, but your mind can still be directed toward it. Now imagine that a word in the story is unfamiliar. You can see the letters without understanding them. Philosophers may ask whether the experience of understanding adds something to consciousness beyond the sounds or images.
summaries.summary: The entry studies consciousness and intentionality as two important but disputed features of the mind. Consciousness is commonly linked with experience: seeing red, hearing a crash, feeling dizzy, recalling an event, imagining a scene, or thinking through a problem all seem to have a subjective side. Intentionality is the mind’s directedness or aboutness. A belief can be about a city, a desire about a future event, and an imagination about a fictional place. The entry warns that both terms are harder to define than they first appear. Not every use of “experience” means the same thing, and philosophers disagree about whether thought is conscious in the same way as sensation. Likewise, intentionality may mean reference to objects, possession of content, or having conditions that make a belief true, a perception accurate, or an intention successful. These ideas become difficult when a person is mistaken, hallucinates, imagines something fictional, or thinks about something nonexistent. Philosophers then ask whether perception and hallucination share a common mental feature or whether genuine perception depends on a real object. The entry surveys phenomenology, which begins with first-person experience and bodily engagement, and analytic philosophy, which often examines language, logic, representation, and mental content. The major disagreement is between separatists and intentionalists. Separatists say conscious feeling can exist independently of aboutness. Intentionalists say conscious experience necessarily involves representation, or that its character can be explained through representational features. key_ideas: Consciousness is often explained through the idea that there is something it is like to have an experience, but philosophers disagree about whether thoughts count as experiences in the same way as sensations.
Intentionality is broader than ordinary “doing something intentionally.” It includes the mind’s directedness in belief, desire, perception, imagination, and thought.
Mental states can be mistaken, unfulfilled, or about nonexistent things, which makes a simple theory of reference difficult.
Some philosophers emphasize the subject’s experience; others argue that perception and thought depend essentially on relations to the body, world, or community.
The debate includes whether perception has a non-conceptual form of intentionality and whether conscious thought has its own distinctive feel.
Theories also disagree about whether consciousness is automatically aware of itself, or whether self-awareness requires a further act of reflection.
summaries.why_it_matters: The relationship between consciousness and intentionality helps determine what counts as a genuine mind rather than a system that merely carries information. It affects how perception can give us knowledge, how we understand our own thoughts, and whether thinking has a distinctive kind of experience. It also connects to questions about artificial minds, the boundaries of the self, and why conscious life may have special value.

important_terms.definition: Having an experience with a subjective feel, such as the way a color, sound, emotion, or thought appears to the person experiencing it.
The feature of a mental state that makes it about or directed toward something.
The information or meaning carried by a belief, desire, perception, or thought; what the state says or represents.
A theory that connects conscious experience with intentionality instead of treating them as wholly separate.
A theory that treats conscious feeling and mental aboutness as distinct features that need not occur together.
The view that mental content is partly fixed by relations to the environment or a person’s language community.
The possibility that consciousness includes awareness of one’s own mental states or of oneself as the subject having them.
The view that thinking and understanding can have an experiential character that is not merely a matter of sounds, pictures, or other sensations.

questions_to_think_about: Can you imagine something that does not exist? What exactly is your imagination about?
Could a person see a shape without understanding what kind of object it is?
Is a hallucination more like genuine perception or more like a thought?
Does noticing your own feeling require a second mental state?
Would a machine that uses information but has no felt experience have a mind?
